utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there is a matter I want to deal with first before we turn to the matters before us today. We have received an additional request, it's called, for allocation of adequate time to prepare a final trial brief on the part of the accused Mr. Cerkez. I thought we made the matter quite plain during the argument; however, we have received yet another document. We said and made it quite plain that we were not going to follow those cases in which more than a month had been granted of time, court time, in order for counsel to prepare their cases, cases which they should be preparing throughout the trial, in this case, one that has gone on for more than 18 months. We made it plain we were not going to follow that practice. We're not going to. We recognise that there have been late disclosure of documents, which has added pressure. Therefore, balancing those matters, we are prepared to add to allow some time. But the point is this: that it is our duty to ensure the trials before this Tribunal are expeditious, and the way to do that is to ensure that submissions and briefs are put in on time. The order that we make for the timetable, having regard to the advancement of witnesses as its been possible, is that all rebuttal and rejoinder evidence will be completed in the week ending the 8th of December. Written briefs will be submitted by Wednesday, 13th December, 4.00 p.m. That will enable the Trial Chamber to have sight of those documents before the arguments on the 14th and 15th. Now, we have received a huge amount of material. We have been considering, in the last half hour, as to what procedure we can follow in order to best assimilate and rule upon it. Having regard to the fact that the transcript witnesses aren't available anyway, that being -- it may be something which can be hived off from the documents. We have in mind to deal with them tomorrow if we permit them to be called and deal with the whole question of transcripts then. We note that there are three witnesses whom the Prosecution proposed to call. We would propose hearing argument in relation to those witnesses as to whether they should be called and ruling upon that and hearing any of the witnesses who we allow to be called. We then turn to the exhibits. I've noted that there are no less than 266. This will require time for consideration. Having heard the witnesses, we will hear oral submissions. We will then, ourselves, go through the documents and rule upon them. If we require additional argument, we will indicate accordingly. I think at the outset one should say this: that for evidence to be admitted after the end of the Prosecution case, particularly at this late stage in the trial, is an extraordinary proceeding and one which can only be contemplated if evidence comes to light which was not available to the Prosecution before the end of the close of its case, could not by reasonable foresight and diligence be obtained, which is in addition relevant and relevant significantly to the trial, going to the core issues and not the peripheral issues in the case. We have in mind that the core issues are, of course, whether the accused are implicated or not in the crimes. So it's against that background that we are going to decide whether to admit any of this evidence and, if so, which. And I would ask this: that we bear in mind two things. We have a duty, of course, to find the truth, if that is possible, but at the same time, we have a duty to ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious, and we have to bear in mind the rights of the accused in that connection. So there is a balancing act which we have to perform in order to decide which, if any, of this evidence we shall admit. In due course, we will formulate the test which we will apply to the exhibits but I make those points at the outset. Now, unless there are any contrary submissions, we will hear first of all the submissions in relation to the three witnesses and then hear the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No contrary submissions as to procedure. Can I simply bring you up to date? There's been an exchange this morning of written arguments which I think will have found their way to the Court but probably haven't yet found their way to Your Honours directly. I'm not sure, or if so, only just; one from us, and one from the Kordic Defence. Those arguments go to the merits, generally, of admission of the Zagreb documents and we would like, obviously, an opportunity, there's no doubt, as with the Defence, to address the Court in respect of those arguments, but it seems that can certainly be postponed until the discreet issue of calling the witnesses is disposed of. It's obviously all related as Mr. Scott, who is going to have the lion's share concerning these arguments on our behalf, says and we are all entirely in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we must adopt a procedure which is orderly; we cannot just allow a free for all. Now, in relation to the witnesses, you have three: Mr. Tomljanovich, Mr. Prelec, and Mr. Bajwa, you propose to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well we've had the opportunity of looking at what it's proposed that they should say. It may be helpful if I indicate what a preliminary view is. Mr. Tomljanovich produces or deals with the obtaining of the material in Zagreb. Potentially that's admissible. He also gives his opinions in relation to the agencies of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, the intelligence agencies. It doesn't seem to me at this stage of the trial that that sort of evidence is going to be admissible. Mr. Prelec, on the other hand, gives rather more detail about the Zagreb material and the obtaining of it. That -- those are matters of fact and, therefore, he is potentially admissible. Mr. Bajwa appears to give a summary of information available to the Office of the Prosecutor relating to the HVO archive. It seems to me that potentially that is not going to be admissible. We don't want or we are not going to be assisted by the opinions of the investigator on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask Mr. Scott perhaps to respond briefly to those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. What I said to Mr. Nice was that all these issues, everything the Chamber has touched on so far this morning, are all clearly interrelated, and what brings us before the Chamber this morning in terms of the presentation of the so-called Zagreb evidence is all one piece in the sense of how it was obtained, why we are where we are. In order to address that, Your Honours, we would seek to make an overall presentation of our position on that which it does, as I said, relate to the position of the witnesses. I can say in general without going into a lot of detail, and I think at some point it may become necessary in order for the Chamber to be fully advised on these issues which relate to matters in Zagreb and outstanding binding orders and requests for assistance, that there be some closed ex parte consideration based upon the Court's knowledge of other prior history in these matters. But let me say for the moment this: One could argue, we don't necessarily concede this position, the Prosecution, but one could argue that there might be other witnesses, so-called firsthand witnesses, if I can use that terminology, to some of these things different than the three individuals proposed by the Prosecutor to call here. The reality is, Your Honours, that despite tremendous efforts, I submit, on behalf of the Prosecution, to bring this evidence before the Chamber in terms of some of the witnesses, some of the names of whom some of you have heard about in the past few days, the past week. The reality is that none of those people have come forward. Summons sought to be served in Croatia to approach these people were not, in fact, served by the Croatian government. None of these people made themselves available to be interviewed. And I think the Chamber has to be aware of that in terms of them considering the steps and actions available to the Prosecutor to bring as much information as possible to the Chamber and to provide as much assistance as possible to the Chamber. I would urge the Chamber to take note of the fact that this is a Tribunal which takes an inclusive rather than exclusive approach or philosophy towards evidence. We frequently hear that there is no rule against hearsay, simply as an example. The Chamber has heard, rightfully so, a large amount of hearsay evidence from all parties and, frankly, I submit, on issues much more closely connected with the guilt or innocence of the accused than the provenance of documents. There seems to be no reason, we would submit, the Prosecution would submit, there is no reason why if hearsay is admissible, even so-called double hearsay is admissible on issues of more core relevance to the case, there is no good reason or policy why hearsay should be excluded coming from witnesses which simply lay foundations for documents that certainly do not have to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. A foundation of a document, the authentication of evidence does not have to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Simply some indicia, some showing has to be made to the Chamber to assist the Chamber in coming to the conclusion that for purposes of authenticity, the document is what it purports to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Scott, might I suggest that what you should concentrate on is the appropriate standing order for admitting evidence at this stage of the trial. We know about the inclusivity approach, but at this stage, what is the standard the Prosecution having closed its case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have to say, Judge Robinson, and to the rest of the Chamber, I would disagree, and I must say I disagree respectfully with the conclusions that were -- or at least the preliminary views that were expressed on that. The Prosecution did not close its case on this very issue and the position that the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Scott, the trial is virtually over and here you are seeking to produce a raft of new documents. I mean, first of all, you must have some consideration to the amount of documentation in a case. A Prosecution simply cannot swamp a Trial Chamber in documents and continue responsibly. That is one matter you've got to consider. The other is that you've got to consider the balance of the trial. The Defence have closed their case, and the fact that you reserved, as you did, your position on these documents doesn't mean that the Trial Chamber has to forget the position in the trial in which you're now seeking to adduce this new evidence. Judge Robinson, of course, is right, that the stage of the trial is a crucial matter to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not dismiss for a moment the difficulties that everyone, all sides, including the Prosecution, has had to deal with with the late availability of this material from Croatia. It is indeed the Prosecutor who has sought this information, this evidence, for years, and was frustrated at every turn, and it was not due to any lack of diligence or lack of effort on the Prosecutor's part that this was available. So I can assure the Chamber, I can ensure the entire Chamber that the Prosecutor, in some respects, has been just as frustrated and finds itself in a difficult situation as much as the Chamber itself, the Registry, the Defence, and everyone involved in this case. The reality is the material was not previously available. To answer one of the Chamber's questions about could -- the nature of this material or its prior availability in the exercise of due diligence. I say in terms of what's been listed on the schedules that have been provided to the Chamber, none of that material was available prior to March 10th. The material was in the hands of the Zagreb government and it was beyond our reach, all of it. Not some, not one or two, not three or four, not a hundred, everything that we have scheduled was beyond our reach as of the 10th of March of this year. We have done everything possible to bring that material to the Chamber as quickly as possible. It is simply, understanding the Chamber's multiple duties, which we fully understand and respect, it is not the Prosecutor's fault and the Prosecutor's case, and in fact, if I may say so, the search for truth and justice in this case should not be penalised by the actions of third parties when they have proven -- provided documentation. That has been completely beyond our control, and I would be prepared again, should the Chamber give us the opportunity and in closed ex parte session, which we are prepared to do a detailed statement as to every step, even in the past 60 to 90 days, of every request, every exchange to get this material to the Chamber as quickly as possible. Some of it was coming as recently as last week, even though we might call literally every day and say, "Where is it?" We've been asking for months; "Where it is?" We have done everything that we can possibly do to bring this evidence, important evidence, before the Chamber. The witnesses, Your Honours, can assist the Chamber in providing background information going to the provenance of the documents and how they relate to the case. I urge again: This evidence is not offered for the purpose of proving any of these propositions necessarily beyond a reasonable doubt. No single piece of evidence, no single witness. That is not the measure of admissibility. Does a document or does a piece of evidence standing alone so overwhelming that it is proof beyond a reasonable doubt? These witnesses are being proposed to the Chamber simply to assist the Chamber, to provide some information and background about certain issues that relate to these documents and can provide that information to the Chamber. The fact that some of it or much of it would be hearsay, I don't think conclusions, I don't think it's necessary to say opinions, observations based on information collected over a substantial period of time and provide that information to the Chamber so that it can understand and rule on this material with as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, for instance, just to take that example, on the intelligence communities, none of that is necessarily to be considered to be establishing any of these propositions once and for all with any great certainty, but the Chamber has heard and will see in the documents much discussion about various of the agencies and who these people are. Who is Ivica Lucic? Why is Ivica Lucic communicating with Miroslav Tudjman, the head of the Croatian information service in Zagreb? Who are some of these people? What are the known relationships or the understood relationships about them? How did the Croatian SIS relate to the Herceg-Bosna SIS? This is information that we submit would be helpful to the Chamber. That's -- would be helpful to the Chamber to assess the evidence and these documents. And we bring, in the absence of these people from Croatia coming forward, and we've sought to summons 15 people, not one appeared, the Republic of Croatia did not serve, to our knowledge, one summons. That leaves us in a situation - my apologies to the interpreters. I don't have my headset on so I'm not getting any message. I give my apology - which we're trying, in the absence of that, to provide the Chamber with as much assistance as possible. And we think the presentations could be, if the Chamber wishes, reasonably brief. They've made their statements, they've provided the information to the Chamber, we're happy to provide them for cross-examination. That's our position on that, Your Honour. We have -- well, Your Honour, again, we have taken every step to prove quickly as possible on these matters. The documents themselves, frankly, the vast majority of these documents are HVO documents. They are no different in nature and kind or substance than the hundreds and hundreds if not thousands at this stage that the Chamber has received from all parties. There simply is no difference. And for some different standard to be applied -- for some different standard to be applied to these virtually identical documents now would be, in our submission, not fair, and both sides and all sides again have submitted these documents, even already. The Defences have submitted HVO documents from Zagreb without producing an authenticating witness, without witnesses. This is a vast category of material which all sides, since April 1999, have submitted to the Chamber, and this material, the vast majority of this material is absolutely no different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in order to be able to gain some time, because we are at a late stage of the trial, you don't need to remind us of everything we know about hearsay evidence, about the provenance of the documents, about the fact that we have had that type of document before, et cetera. You don't need to repeat all that. Where you can help us, where you can be of assistance to the Chamber is by telling us at this stage, i.e., as the President has reminded you, 18 months after the beginning of the trial, what you can tell us at this stage is amongst these 260 documents. Amongst these 260 documents, what are the documents that considering all the other documents we have seen, all the evidence we have heard, what are the documents amongst these documents that you deem absolutely essential, absolutely necessary, considering the criteria that have been reminded to you? What are the documents that are new, that are essential, that are relevant? What are the documents that can have an impact on the guilt of the accused? If you can tell us on that particular point, I think you would help us moving ahead, and that's where we want to hear you. We don't want to hear any type of general submissions because really, it's not the time to -- for us to hear that type of thing because we've heard that sort of submissions many, many times before and we have decisions of the Appeals Chamber about that type of question. So as professional Judges, we know all that. But it would be better if you could help us, as Judge Robinson has said, to tell us at this stage of the trial why you believe that such and such documents should be admitted as evidence in order to bring out the truth, because what we are looking for here is to move towards the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, what you can do is this: Rather than general submissions as the Judge has said, we will, in due course, want particular submissions about documents. And so if you would like to be thinking and preparing as to which of the documents you particularly rely on, we will hear you in due course. Which, as it were, out of the 260 of the 20 you rely on or something of that sort and you can turn your mind to that while we deal with the rest of the evidence. Is there anything more you want to say about these three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I can just respond to your last point. I mean we will, obviously, take the Court's guidance as we always do, and give that further consideration. I think -- I have to say it's difficult, because when the Chamber obviously gets these documents, you get some, as you say, 260 documents, obviously that looks like a lot and by some measure, 260 documents is a lot. On the other hand, Your Honours, if you will allow me for a moment, please, to say that when you have, in the past six months, seen literally hundreds of thousands of documents, literally, with no exaggeration, hundreds of thousands of documents and you cut and you cut and you select and you select and you get down to 260 documents which is probably something less than one per cent, we have been extremely selective. We have been extremely selective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have no doubt you have been. I have no doubt it's extremely frustrating having decided that these were the ones on which you were going to rely to be told or to asked on which ones you rely on. Your answer is: I rely on them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is which are the ones you particularly rely on, that's what we want to know. But we'll hear argument about the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, on behalf of Mr. Kordic, let me just say this. While we were preparing for the cross-examination of these three witnesses at issue this weekend, and as we were considering the arguments to be made in opposing parts of their testimony, we received, you might confidently predict, the usual huge quantity of new documents that we have been receiving on an almost daily basis for the last few months. These documents here were the new documents in addition to the ones that Mr. Kovacic has on his desk which we lacked the manpower and muscle power to bring over today, but I'm glad he has. In addition to these documents, we've received indices. Apparently, the Kordic indices has grown from 13 pages to 25 pages. One final comment on that, Your Honour, the physical magnitude of the documents themselves that you've just seen doesn't really need any further explanation. We merely ask the Court to apply its order of October 4th that required a final Zagreb materials submission, a final one, by October 30th. Now, with respect to these three witnesses, we have no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will hear, in due course, which documents were supplied after the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that's why I just wanted to make the point and I am departing from it. You've asked about these three witnesses, let me address them in turn. Mr. Bajwa appears to be the clean-up witness. The one who's going to express his belief, essentially, that the documents that he has seen consist of the HVO archive that was referred to in Dr. Prlic's March 25th, 1993 decision. Pure opinion, absolutely undiluted speculation and conjecture on his part and we object to that. We don't object to him, obviously, testifying what he's done, what he's seen, the people even to whom he's spoken. That's not opinion testimony. That's within his competence as a fact witness, and if he has any valuable insights to offer in that regard then maybe we should hear them. Turning to Mr. Tomljanovich. He's given not one, but two statements. As the Court knows, he's -- he talks about first of all what he's seen, what he's read, how it was produced. No problem with any of that. Then he goes on to give his views about the various Croatian secret service agencies and espionage agencies with apparently no basis disclosed in the statement that he's provided for any expertise in that regard. There's no indication given to us or the Trial Chamber that he has the slightest expertise to talk about the inner workings of secret service and espionage agencies or indeed whether he's ever spoken to anybody connected with them. We most respectfully object to any opinions of that type; they are not helpful. It's just undiluted expert testimony and he's not really even been identified, I think, formally as an expert even though one could presume that that's the capacity in which he's proffered, and just to be careful, we've filed a Rule 94 bis (B)(ii) notice just to be safe. So we object to the things covered by his second statement, the matters of expert testimony regarding secret service agencies. In so far as Mr. Prelec is concerned, he gives seemingly factual testimony about what he's seen, what he's read, the people to whom he's spoken. We have no problem with that, but we do have a problem with paragraph 15 of his proposed statement where he proposes to tip toe into Your Honour's province and utter opinions regarding the general consistency of all of the documents that he's seen, the kinds of things that are necessary in order to lay the foundation required by the Delalic decision of March 4 of 1998 referred to in our papers and a copy of which we provided to you earlier today. That's not for him to say. That's for you to say. And he is not here to assess the internal content of those documents and whether they're consistent with the evidence you've heard but, of course, he can talk about what he's seen, the people to whom he's spoken and what he's read. Opinions of the type in paragraph 15, however, are not helpful and they are not within his competence and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters but I've finished my presentation. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, we are joining all the arguments explained by our colleagues from Kordic Defence. However, I would like to add only two or three words. I will not waste the time of this Court and I will continue in Croatian language. [Interpretation] These documents from so-called Zagreb archives are arriving in huge quantities and have been arriving for the past two months. However, one thing is very important. We see from those documents that their disclosure could have started much earlier. Many of these documents could have been accorded foundation through some witnesses who were still in the courtroom at the time, I mean Defence witnesses. Some of the key witnesses who could speak about key documents were in the courtroom at the time when the Prosecution evidently did have those documents but did not produce them. This transpires from the information of proposed Prosecution witnesses, and there is a clear information there that most of the documents from the Vitez Brigade files which the Prosecutors went through in Zagreb arrived in Zagreb much earlier than it is being shown at present. Later disclosure of those documents, that is, is not therefore only the product of objective circumstances but, to a great extent, the result of the Prosecution's tactic. I should like to point out two other things that I believe are of consequence. First, regarding the number itself, and I cannot quote the exact number, but there is quite a large number of documents and it should be pointed out that they were either issued by Cerkez or officers directly subordinate to him at the time covered by the indictment referring to the then turned situation not covering something that happened before that. So what are these documents, daily orders, daily reports which absolutely have no value in terms of a look backward and these are documents which were, perhaps, issued in November or December 1993 or even perhaps documents of the Vitez Brigade dating to January 1994. That is not only that it goes beyond the period of the indictment, but it is at that time when Cerkez was not even the commander. So what is the purpose of those documents? Their purpose is only to create an atmosphere, to create an environment in which the Prosecution can then skillfully use the documents that they need and they technically deferred their production. The purpose was not the truth. The second thing I wish to say is these are documents, and we gradually came to realise that from, I should call it curious information, from various offices in these cases. Some of it is going intimated through different documents, some of this was in the live testimony, but these documents were in the possession of at least three different information services over a period of not less than six years. We could see from some objective signs that intelligence services which had conflicting interests and that they even contained some departments within them with conflicting interests. I believe that in the world of intelligence it is a promise land for the fabrication of documents, and I am confident that there are some documents which were fabricated, and we shall go into that when we reach the rejoinder case. But it is a fact that three intelligence services had these documents that they criss-crossed half of Bosnia and half of Croatia on their way to different places, and we really have no way of establishing which way is authentic and which is not. That is why I think that unless the Defence challenges the authenticity of individual documents, then -- no, I was wrong, excuse me. But as soon as the Defence challenges the authenticity of individual documents, that document loses all its property value because it lacks the foundation and because we cannot see the original and there is no doubt that there is a climate when some documents were used or fabricated in different ways or planted on individual services. I have nothing against documents, but we have never received from the Prosecution a proposal, a proposed list which documents we could agree upon and which we couldn't. We did not do it and there are quite a number of documents which are in dispute. That is all that I wish to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered these submissions. We broadly agree with the Defence submissions as far as these matters are concerned. We bear in mind the stage of the trial which we're at, which I've already referred to in argument, that is, after the close of the Defence case. Therefore, there can only be a limited right to call witnesses at that time. We regard the evidence of Mr. Prelec as admissible because he deals with the recovery of these documents and those are matters of fact on which he's entitled to give evidence. We agree, however, with the submission about paragraph 15. Those are matters for argument by counsel, not by a witness. We will admit Mr. Prelec. In those circumstances, we do not think that Mr. Tomljanovich is necessary. The first part of his evidence is covered in much more detail by Mr. Prelec, and we don't need to have it repeated by Mr. Tomljanovich. The second part are matters of opinion which, at this stage of the trial, are inadmissible. Likewise, Mr. Bajwa, we do not think his evidence to be admissible at this stage. These are summaries of information available to the Prosecutor. They are matters of opinion. We will hear Mr. Prelec at half past eleven. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to take a seat, Mr. Prelec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, let me start at the -- if I'll be allowed, just in terms of your background to summarise the statement you prepared some time ago, and I should say that -- do you recall that on approximately -- on the 29th of October this year, 2000, a statement was prepared and bears your signature on page 8? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were born in Zagreb, Croatia, were you not, in 1966?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You came -- your family came to the United States in 1967, accepted American citizenship in 1977. After an undergraduate education at Harvard you completed a doctorate in history at Yale in 1997. Your specialisation in these studies was the modern history of Yugoslavia, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, that's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You thereafter taught at several colleges and universities for two years after receiving your doctorate. You most recently, prior to coming to the OTP, had taught at the United States Naval Academy. In May of 1999 you took up your present post at a research office with the OTP at the International Tribunal, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and the witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, we both speak sometimes quickly, and because we speak the same language, we don't leave a break between the question and answer. So both of us perhaps could be reminded of a short pause for translation.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Thank you for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as an historian, as a trained historian, is it correct to say that you have worked in archival environments, if you will, on a number of occasions, both during and after your education?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as I understand it, sir, and as you have stated in your statement, you have worked, in fact, in archives in Zagreb and Zadar, Croatia; in Vienna, Austria; Ljubljana, Slovenia, and also in Washington, D.C., the United States; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I've worked in all those places in archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just ask you briefly, sir. Your position as a research officer at the OTP, what does that involve? I'm sure the Chamber would only appreciate a brief answer, but just what do you do as a research officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: The simple answer is I do research in the documentary collections maintained by the Office of the Prosecutor, and I also do research in other documentary collections to which this institution has access. Most recently, those were archives in Zagreb, Croatia. So I look for documents and I attempt to subject them to historical understanding that allows me to piece together a treatment of the institutions of the states of the former Yugoslavia not just with reference to crime, but simply in a non-controversial way with reference to the various institutions that existed there, how they functioned in law and in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that in your work as an historian and someone working in archives, does the nature of your work involve looking at more than a single document in isolation or do you attempt to look at a range or body of documents and come to some analysis or certain conclusions about the material that you review?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I always look at, if I can, documents in the context in which they come to me. If one -- it's very difficult to treat or to understand a document in isolation if one doesn't know where it comes from or their circumstances, but when one has the opportunity to review a large collection, there are things that become commonsensically apparent that would not otherwise be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention now, then, please, specifically to the access gained by the Office of the Prosecutor to a collection of documents that has become known as the HVO archive or referred to as the HVO archive in Zagreb or around Zagreb and I direct your attention, for purposes of starting this area, if you will, on the 2nd of May, 2000. Can you confirm to the Chamber that it was on approximately May 2nd of this year that the OTP first gained access to some of the documents making up the HVO archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you describe to the Chamber just what the procedures and steps -- the procedures that were followed and the steps taken in accessing and reviewing this material in that early period?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: There was a series of negotiations between officers of the Office of the Prosecutor and representatives of the government of Croatia to which I was not entirely privy. I can personally testify to our first actual encounter or our first actual access to the documents in question which took place at a house owned by the government of Croatia in the suburb of Samobor. We were taken to this house by persons we understood to be working in one of the police or, not to be too dramatic, secret police services of the government of Croatia. There, we were shown a crate of approximately 20 binders full of documents which had been -- which all concerned the area of Central Bosnia in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, at that particular time, did you know or come to know about that time which agency or arm or branch of the Croatian government physically possessed this collection of documents at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the HIS which was the Croatian Information Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Chamber, please, your basis for saying that how do you know that those documents at that time were in possession of HIS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, it was common knowledge. It was, I suppose, personally confirmed to me at a slightly later date when I had occasion to meet the gentleman who was the director of the HIS and discuss with him ongoing access to the materials in question which, I think, demonstrates that they were, in fact ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this individual that you've just described, was that Dr. Ozran Zunec who was, during the first six months of this year, approximately, following the establishment of the new government, the director of the HIS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure exactly how long his tenure was, but it was in the early part of this year and, yes, it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the record on this point is clear, the director, the senior, the number one official of HIS confirmed to you at that time this HVO archive was in the possession and under the control of HIS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the witness should not be led through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't lead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, will you go back to the time when you were at this house in Samobor, and what was the process by which the documents would actually be reviewed and, if they were, copies requested?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, we were in a large room with usually two representatives of the government of Croatia. I personally took them to be some sort of security officers, always at least one there with us. And we would simply take the binders of documents and read them in the morning. In the afternoon, another representative of the government would arrive with blank forms, blank numbered forms that he would give us, and we were instructed to fill out these forms with the pertinent information of the documents we wished to have copied. We would do this and submit them to him and the copies would be delivered to us through the Office for Cooperation with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And before moving on to the receipt of the copies back, who did you understand or what did you understand the Office for Cooperation to be? What function did it have in the Croatian government if you know, and how was it related to the work that you were doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: There is nothing mysterious about this. It's a public organ of the government of Croatia that is responsible for coordinating relations between that government and the ICTY and the ICJ. They respond to binding orders. They arrange visits. They respond to requests for assistance and the like. They've been dealing with this institution for some years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I mention this only because it may connect with the Chamber's experience with an individual or two that the Chamber has seen here in the courtroom. Is one of the individuals, perhaps the head of that Office for Cooperation, is that a man named Orsat Miljenic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljenic is the head of that office. I have met him on several occasions in an official capacity, in that official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may be worth staying on that point for just a moment longer. Do you understand that in addition to or above the Office for Cooperation there is something called a council which is also involved in overseeing and making decisions, if you will, on cooperation with the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. This is also publicly known. It's a publicly known aspect of Croatian law. I'm not sure when exactly the council to which you refer came into being, but it has existed at all times that I have had dealings with the Office for Cooperation. It consists of a number of high officials. Its president is the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Goran Granic, and Mr. Zunec, was, during his tenure, I believe, also a member of that council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, does that also include the Minister of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I believe it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when you would request documents of those reviewed, you would get copies back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. We would get copies from the office. In this period while we were working in Samobor, we would get copies from the Office for Cooperation. On at least two occasions, the very first and one subsequent one, I personally took delivery from the Office for Cooperation, once from Mr. Miljenic and once from one of his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me ask you, during that time period specifically, did you have any understanding that the documents -- copies of the documents requested by the Prosecution, the Office of the Prosecutor, were being also made available to various Defence teams, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: We were told -- I was told that the arrangement -- I was told this by, among others, Mr. Zunec. The arrangement was every copy that we received would also be given to the Defence and copies requested by the Defence, in those words, would also be given to us. And I can confirm this in at least two respects. On one occasion I waited for several hours in the office, and finally a man came with two boxes of copies. I had been expecting a large delivery, and I thought they were -- both boxes were for me and I wanted both of them, and he said, "No. One of them is for you and the other is an identical set for the Defence. You may have whichever one you wish," and it was, in fact, a complete copy. I subsequently saw documents that were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor that had been selected or were represented as having been selected by various attorneys representing various defendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the general question or topic of receiving the copies back, can you tell the Chamber, were steps normally taken or regularly taken to inspect or to verify that the copies received were, in fact, the copies of the documents which had been requested?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, such steps were taken. On the first delivery, I inspected the copies right there in the Office for Cooperation. As the deliveries grew larger, this became cumbersome and they were generally inspected at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: But yes. The brief answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for counsel and the Chamber, we're on paragraph -- roughly paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that this -- again, this early period of access to the HVO documents in Samobor continued for approximately eight working days and then there were some interruptions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I believe it was seven days. I'm not sure. There were two distinct interruptions. I'm not sure to which you refer, but, yes, there was a period of roughly seven days, after which we were told that the facility we used, the house in Samobor, would be hosting representatives of the Defence. We were given a date, some days off, when we could resume work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know in part, again because of meetings with Mr. Zunec and others, that the reason for this interruption or delay was because various Defence counsel were being provided at that time access to this material?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, this is what he said. It was awkward, because we had been told that we could resume work on a particular date in May. I forget precisely what that date was. When we arrived in Zagreb with a small team to resume work, we were told, immediately after arrival, that no, we would have to wait longer because the Defence was still working. And we met with -- I met with a number of other people, with Mr. Zunec in the premises of the Office for Cooperation. I attempted to persuade him to allow us to have continued access in some other way, perhaps at a different facility or access to a different part of the collection. I offered many compromises, all of which were declined at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving on then. On approximately the 22nd of May, as I understand it, the OTP was again allowed or was allowed to start again the review of this material; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber how long that period, if you will, that period of review lasted?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: It lasted one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of why the work came to an end at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: It was actually quite dramatic. I received a call - I believe it was late on the evening of that day - from a [redacted] of the Zagreb field office, informing me that we would not be working the next day because a newspaper in Croatia had published an article reviewing the details of our inspection of the archive, complete with photographs of the house in which we were working, names of HIS agents who had been assisting us. I saw that newspaper the next morning and it did, in fact, have those things in it. So we waited throughout the morning in our hotel. We were told that -- we were accompanied by HIS agents who were seeing who else would come, but it became, subsequently, for this reason, impossible to resume work at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that that or continuing difficulties, if I could put it this way, continuing difficulties with accessing and reviewing these materials resulted in Prosecutor Del Ponte and Deputy Prosecutor Blewitt travelling to Zagreb with others on the 24th [Realtime transcript read in error "4th"] of May with the Prime Minister Racan, the Deputy Prime Minister Goran Granic, and the Minister of Justice Stjepan Ivanisevic to discuss issues and problems with the OTP gaining access and having access to this material?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I can confirm that. I was in Zagreb at the time as sort of a place holder, and I met Deputy Prosecutor Blewitt at the airport. I did not meet the Prosecutor herself, but I saw her get off the plane and into her limousine. So yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A correction in the transcript, Your Honour. The place where it says the "4th of May" should be the "24th of May."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you come to know then, Mr. Prelec, that after this time -- sometime after this meeting, with among others the Prosecutor and the Prime Minister, that an alternative or a solution was found by which this HVO archive would be moved and instead of being reviewed at the -- in parts, perhaps I should say, being reviewed in parts at Samobor, this safe house, that instead the collection would be moved to the Croatian State Archive which is actually located in what might be called downtown or central Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you come to understand that as part of these arrangements, that Defence -- various Defence counsel would also continue to have the same, in fact, exactly the same access to the material as the Office of the Prosecutor did?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: This was said to us immediately and that part of the reason for moving the collection to the Croatian State Archive was because that facility had -- was better able to host both representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and representatives of the Defence simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were there times, in fact, during -- when you were in Zagreb conducting this work that you, yourself, saw and perhaps at times even interacted with various Defence counsel who were at the archive looking at these documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I did see representatives of -- well, I did see Defence attorneys, few of whom I recognised, but some I did recognise. I did not, as far as I recall, interact with them. For most of the time, they were in an adjacent room. However, there were several occasions on which we had to share a room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, just in terms of the time frame, for the Chamber to understand the period over which this exercise was primarily carried out, is it fair to say that from the time we are talking about now that most of the work in the archive took place between approximately June and the latter part of September of this year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. It continued after that period, but I would say the most intense portion was the summer months you describe, and I was present there working for most of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when you first started work, and this even goes back to the time when you were still at the house in Samobor, can you tell the Chamber, please, did you have any indices or inventory or list of documents available to assist you in reviewing or choosing the material to be reviewed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I don't recall any indices at the house in Samobor, but either immediately or very soon after beginning work at the Croatian State Archive in June, indices were made available to us in the room we worked in. They were initially incomplete. We were told by archival staff -- I was told by archival staff that they were actually producing them as we were working, and they would periodically give me and others updated catalogues or indices. These were basically lists of binders, some just with titles, some with short descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At that particular time, and I realise that the collection, the size of the collection changed over time, and we will address that with the Chamber in the course of your testimony but, again, directing your attention primarily to the June time period, June/July, perhaps, what did you understand the total volume, approximately, of the volume of material that was being stored as part of the archive at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Initially, several people told me that it was on the order of 2.000 binders. I -- one of the first days I was in the Croatian State Archive, I spoke with the director of that institution, Mr. Josip Kulenovic, and I asked him if I could see the actual collection, and he agreed to take me there. It was in the basement in a large room and it was, indeed, quite large. It was -- I did not count each individual binder but it seemed to be that much or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just so the record is clear, when you say "binder", you're talking something like a notebook or something like I'm holding up here?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So at that particular time, at least 2.000 of these binders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you just describe to the Chamber, since the Chamber has not had the opportunity to see this collection itself, just describe to the Chamber what this material looked like, especially on the occasion or occasions when you were actually able to see the entire collection. What did it look like? What was the condition of it? How was it arranged? Just give the Chamber, please, an idea of what this collection was like.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, I only saw the entire collection once. It was a long row of compact shelves, in other words, shelves that had to -- you had to work a little mechanism to create an aisle between them. Most of it appeared to be binders sort of arranged, you know, from one row to the next. There were also some materials that were in stacks of loose or not loose paper but stacks of paper bound with a ribbon or something. There were also boxes of material. There was also one of the trunks that the HIS staff had used to convey material to Samobor. That was still there. We got back to that trunk, the one we had been working on in the last day. We got back to that sometime later. But the majority of at least what I saw consisted of binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of the contents of the binders, the documents themselves, what kind of documents did you see? And just to make my question a bit more clearer, such things as faxes, was there computer printouts? What kind of material did you see?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: There was a large variety. There were faxes. I didn't like these, because many of them had faded. They were printed on thermal paper. Some of them were very difficult to read. Others were slightly better preserved. There were original documents or what appeared to be original documents. And by that I mean they were on coloured letterhead with a pen signature. There were photocopies of the same. There were things that had printed, or appeared to have been printed on a computer, various kinds of computers. There were handwritten documents, loose pages, notebooks, and diaries. There were restaurant receipts and bills. Thematically, the bulk of what I saw consisted of two kinds of things: orders, military orders, and military reports. Orders being submitted to subordinates, and orders being issued generally to superiors although sometimes they were informational documents that were sent as notice to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did some of the material, and I'm not saying all of it by any means, but did some of the material appear to have been arranged in some order in terms of there was some logical connection within a binder or within some part of the collection?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: In principle it was all arranged, almost all. So, for example, one might find a binder that would be marked "Main Staff of the HVO", "outgoing mail", just citing, as an example, January through March of a certain year. And generally, most of the time, they were arranged in chronological order, although sometimes for no reason they would go reverse chronological order. There were a very small number that were effectively randomly arranged but, yes, they were all thematically somehow arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As a further example, for instance, would you see binders that were marked on the spine "Vitez Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were there other brigades, names of other brigades again that were mentioned on the binders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Actually if I could correct my previous answer, there is a technicality, but I remarked Viteska Brigade in the ZP Vitez. I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Certainly. And did you see a similar binder for other brigades? We talked about Viteska Brigade, but did you see for other -- identified as related to other brigades?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. Stjepan Tomasevic, Nikola Subic-Zrinjski. There may have been others. There were -- it was a great number of brigades that I saw in the catalogues. I'm trying to restrict my answer to ones that I looked at personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of paragraph 9, I think if I might be allowed, based on what the witness has said so far, just simply confirms that copying the ongoing request and copy procedure, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Mr. Prelec, that the basic process continued to be the same and that is that documents would be reviewed for a certain period of time, selections would be made and the selections would be communicated to the archive staff, and then copies would come back to the OTP at various times?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. It became somewhat more efficient. We were allowed to produce our order forms on computer and to make note of what we had been reading, but basically the system was the same. The only, I suppose, significant difference would be that the copies would be handed over to us in the archive by the archival staff as opposed to previously when they had been handed over by the Office for Cooperation. And this allowed us to check them for completeness which we generally did, and to request additional copies if the archive had, in some cases, failed to provide a requested document. It happened seldom, but it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And are you generally familiar with the fact that at various points in time, then, the copied documents would be transmitted back to the Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me address one point that's been raised, and I suppose now is as good a time as any. Could you tell the Chamber, please, starting from the beginning in Samobor, was there always the practice of placing a stamp on the documents, somewhere on the face of the document saying something, obviously in Croatian, about it being the Zagreb or archive collection?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, none of the documents that we reviewed in Samobor or at least none of those that -- none of the copies provided to us by the Office for Cooperation, based on our review in Samobor, had a stamp because it had nothing to do with the Croatian State Archive. I was surprised and pleased when the archive began using this stamp. It seemed to lend a degree of officiality to the process, and they used it most of the time. There were a few occasions when, through what I suspect is an inadvertent omission, they had failed to use that. There were also a few occasions or, rather, I should say at least one occasion when I asked for immediate copies of documents I felt to be especially urgent, and on that occasion they were made in the little Xerox machine in the director's office. I don't recall whether or not those had the stamp, but I could easily imagine that they might not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. But it's fair to say, sir, that the practice of using a stamp is something that developed over time and while, in fact, there came to be a time when it was used most of the time, it was still not all the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. I would stand by my previous answer. Yes, it was used the majority of the time; at the archive though, only there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to direct your attention to August. Did you come to know that in about August that additional documents began to be placed at the state archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- I was notified by again the archival staff that was working in the room that I and my team were using that they had been in receipt of material from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and that they were incorporating this material into their catalogues. They showed me one of the new updated catalogues they had received and showed me how to distinguish new material from old. There had been some concern that they would simply fold it in thematically, but they made clear that no, this material would be preserved separately so that -- well, I'm probably getting into too much detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. I think the point was worth making. To distinguish it from the material that had been previously reviewed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. My particular concern was if they had put it in with -- you know, in an unmarked way, then it would be necessary to duplicate the work that I and others had already done now looking for newly added material. So we requested them to segregate it in some way, at least in different binders, and they readily agreed to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to direct your attention, without leading you too much except to direct you to this topic. Did there come a time around August when this new material was added to the archive, when you came to certain conclusions or made certain observations about the relationship between new material, if I can use that term, and some of the material you had seen before?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. This was probably the most exciting thing that happened to me there. I just, as a trial, I suppose, a trial run, requested access to one of the new boxes that had arrived from the Ministry of Defence. I say as a trial because it was simply marked "ZP Vitez," various things, various units. And when it arrived, and it arrived immediately, as they generally did, I opened it and saw that this consisted of about 20 paper folders, which I flipped through, and I noticed that these folders were marked with the same markings or what seemed to me at the time, and I later confirmed this, the same markings as some of the Central Bosnian binders we had reviewed right at the very beginning in Samobor. Some of these were quite distinctive. They were codes, that were meaningless to me, of seven or eight numbers, and they were indeed identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Okay. I then began to read through these, and I realised very quickly that the material was not the same as what I had reviewed earlier. I'm not claiming my memory is that perfect, but the small number of documents that was in each of these binders - they were quite small - was very striking, and I'm certain I would have recalled. Many of them had to do, for example, with the events on and around the 16th of April of 1993, and these had been very few and far between in the Samobor materials. So I can't say that there was absolutely no overlap, but I'm certain that a large number of those materials had not been in the binders that at least I had reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you able to tell by physically looking at these documents -- did they appear to you to have been documents that at one time had been part of the same collection?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: There was nothing physical about them that would distinguish them from the materials that had been in the other binders or, indeed, any of the binders in the archive. My conjecture was that they had been separated out at one point, that originally they had been where they had been created. So, for example, documents of the Zrinjski Brigade had been with the Zrinjski Brigade, and some of them, especially embarrassing ones, had been --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to the conjecture being offered by the witness in this regard, Your Honour. This verges on speculation. I have sat down and been fairly tolerant before making the objection, but I think that he should be able to testify to what he saw, what he read, people that he spoke to, rather than giving us conjectures and speculations about whether materials were separated out by some unknown person at some unknown point in time. And also, he can't even tell us who put the original binders together, let alone whether these documents were part of those original binders. So I think that this is verging on speculation and conjecture. Actually not verging into it. It's well into that territory, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness can do is give evidence of what he himself saw as far as the documents were concerned, what he had seen beforehand, and what these new documents were. Beyond that, I think there must be force in Mr. Sayers' submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two points before moving on to the next paragraph. Just so the record is clear, and I'm sure the Chamber will know, but when you made reference a moment ago to the 16th of April, 1993, would it be fair to say that some of these particular documents that you began to see and the reason they caught your attention, among other things, was that they had to do with the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Several of the documents in that very box did have to do with Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, if you know, before we move on, is the -- another intelligence service called the Security Information Service or SIS, is that part of the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is, again, publicly known in Croatia. It's not a secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct you then, moving forward, to a particular document that you came across. And I'll just say for the record, and it's not a secret, that it's now been marked as Exhibit Z692.2. Do you recall coming across the document on the -- dated the 16th of April, 1993, information sent by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic to Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I recall seeing a document that bore those names as -- well, the name of Colonel Blaskic was at the bottom in the signatory position, and the name of Mr. Cerkez was at the top in the addressee position. I held it in my hand. On the back, it - and I will doubt I will ever forget this - there were handwritten notes in pencil, very brief notes, listing four Central Bosnian villages, including the village of Ahmici, and in each one, there were a few words describing what was happening there of the nature progressing or running into resistance or things of that nature. As I recall the document, the text of the document had to do with some type of inquiry about what had been happening in those villages. And actually, I later found a report, and my memory fails as to precisely what, but basically retyping the content of those penciled notes in a more typical or conventional format.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: This is one of the ones I requested for immediate copying in the director's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on that occasion, and could some questions come up in the course of the proceedings about the original of that document, and again so the record is clear, you saw the original with the penciled notes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct. And I also checked the copy as it came off the copier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention forward, please, to the HVO archive more generally. Can you relate to the Court at this time what information you had and, to your knowledge, the people you were working with at the time, about the existence, and that is the historical existence, of an HVO archive, and can you just summarise that information to the Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just make one objection, and that is to the second sentence of paragraph 12 of this summary, in light of the Court's prior rulings excluding the testimony of the witness referred to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will ask to be heard on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well, if you lay the foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your work with these materials and having an interest in the HVO archives, sir, did you ever have occasion to review the testimony of General Blaskic. When I say the testimony, his testimony here in The Hague or summaries of that testimony where he discussed his access to the HVO archive in late 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I consulted the LiveNote computer programme version of General Blaskic's testimony. I was actually looking for something else that he discussed immediately after mentioning the archive, but he did or at least the text of the transcript indicated that he had said that he had reviewed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think this is where we get into controversial matter. Now, Mr. Scott, you want to address us. How are we going to be assisted by this information anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the assistance is, Your Honour, that it was General Blaskic's testimony in his own case and this is not being -- this is not an effort to bring in wholesale his literally days and weeks of testimony on central issues to the case, but simply as it relates to the provenance of HVO documents and his own knowledge of having been to the archive in late 1995 in Siroki Brijeg and reviewing a number of documents there, in fact, including some of his own documents. And that's the only purpose for which it's offered at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Scott, we are against you. This is effectively bringing Mr. Blaskic's evidence in this case, and we're not going to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you, in part of your work in Zagreb with the archive collection, come across information within the archive itself which gave you insights, if you will, provided you information about the history of that collection?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, there were numerous or I shouldn't say numerous, there were several things that I found in the archive that bore on the question of HVO documentation and its management. In some ways, the most interesting one was a binder consisting of a large number of photographs of what appeared to be boxes of binders, other binders and each one of these was labelled "Siroki Brijeg, July", in Croatian, "July 1996." And I recall wondering whether this was, in fact, the very archive I was looking at. Many of the binders were photographed in a way that did not allow one to see their spine, but at least one or two, and I didn't make a real photo-by-photo inspection. At least one or two were binders whose spines I recognised from the archive. There were other things that I found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment, please. I apologise for interrupting, but before you move on, the particular material where you found the 150 photographs, can you just tell the Chamber in what -- was there some identification on that binder or on that collection where you found the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Perhaps I should explain that the Croatian State Archive divided this entire collection into about 20 subcategories and this was in the subcategory devoted to the Security and Information Service of the HVO. That consisted of roughly, as I recall, just over 500 binders. It was in that collection. I don't know if that's what you were asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Now, apart from seeing particular binders or the spines of binders, did you see anything in the photographs that indicated a location and time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, on the photos themselves, no. They were glued or attached in some way to sheets of paper all of which said Siroki Brijeg and then it said "FEAL" and I did not know, and still do not know what that means, "July 1996". But the photos themselves were just photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- excuse me a moment. Related to this question, did you come across a document, an SIS document dated about January of 1997 saying anything about this document, and if you recall that, can you explain that to the Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. This was also very interesting. I found in a binder I had ordered by mistake, I had transposed a number. The collection is numbered so in ordering one would say you know, "I want SIS binder number 200 and something." And I went through this binder briefly and I found a security report dated -- at some point in January 1997 from a man named as I recall, Zvonko Sesar, describing SFOR or IFOR activity in his area and specifically mentioning the concern that SFOR or IFOR might seize the archive, the HVO archive, for the purposes or for the use of some international institution, did not specify which one, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the best evidence of what this document says is the document itself, and I believe I'm not incorrect in saying that this has not been provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about to hand out a packet of documents that relate to the balance of this witness' testimony. If I could have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me withdraw the objection. My assistant tells me it was provided, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I believe it's the last in the bundle, if you could put on the ELMO Exhibit 2709.1. Start briefly with the first page and then we'll move on. Mr. Nice reminds me, if it assists in the Chamber in the review that it's been doing of the documents, this is also in the so-called Cerkez bundle of exhibits or miscellaneous, my mistake, miscellaneous bundle of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that, sir, is this -- looking at this document which is 2709.1, does this appear to be the document that you were telling us about a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: May I examine the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It's possible that I had conflated two documents, but this one I do recognise, in my earlier answer, but this one I do recognise as seeing in the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could place the third overall page of the document and just focus for a moment on the middle of that page. It's the portion that says, "In order to protect the war archive material of the HVO units --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Scott, what is the purpose of this? This is a document in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are trying events in 1993. We are swamped, as I have said, with documentation yet you've produced more. Now, the fact that somebody wanted to keep these documents away from SFOR may or may not be the case. How does it assist proving the case against these two accused? You're not suggesting that they were involved in this, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The suggestion is, Your Honour, the reason we were trying to assist the Chamber was that this would help to explain how these documents came from Bosnia to be located in Zagreb. But with the Court's comments, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not disputed, as far I can see, that these documents were not available to you until earlier this year. That being so, it seems to me there is no issue on the point as to how you got them, whether people were withholding them. All that sort of issue which, of course, goes to your attempts to get the material, none of that is, it seems to me, pertinent to the issue of whether or not we should admit the material. That issue has to be determined now since, as I understand, availability is not in dispute, that has to be determined on relevance and fairness to the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
