utterances.text: We have just considered the point. If there is some relevance in this that arises from cross-examination then, of course, you can have the opportunity of going into it. But for the moment, I'm -- I don't think we are assisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you see -- let me just ask you one question. I don't know whether it falls within the Court's range of concerns or not, but moving to paragraph 13, if I can hopefully maybe cover it with one question. Did you see, among the archives, the documents that you were reviewing, evidence that in fact other persons had worked with these documents in connection with cases and investigations before the Tribunal, before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The bulk of the material concerning the use of the archive by persons in one way or another -- well, they were simply referred to as "defence" that I saw personally had to do with interviews that had been arranged and also information on various Prosecution witnesses. But there was some reference to documents and access to them by those same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inquire what the relevance of that particular question is if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The only point that I was making, Your Honour, was: Is the suggestion that this Defence team had access to those materials?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a different point. Mr. Prelec, can you help us as to any indication that there might have been on the documents or any information connected with them as to which Defence team had had access to the documents? Anything that you saw rather than anything you may have heard or rumour or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I can answer the question, Your Honour, in regard to documents that I saw. There were references that I recall to a Mr. Nobilo. The bulk that I saw were there and there were also references to one of the attorneys involved here but in connection to another defendant that he had represented. I don't know if you want me to go into more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unless the Chamber wants to, Your Honour, I'm happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think I take the point. Defence counsel in connection with another case.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's precisely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, anybody who wants to ask any questions about that can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention now to specifically a particular -- again, a particular exhibit that you came across, and can you just tell the Chamber, in your own words, an inquiry that you made concerning a particular Blaskic order? If I can introduce the matter that way. Without leading you further, can you just tell the Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, some time ago, I was asked by one of the -- well, by Mr. Nice to examine a document. This was a -- something presented as a -- or as a preparatory combat order. It was -- I was told it had been presented in another case and also in this case. It had a date and a time, that date being the 15th of April. The time, I believe, unless I'm conflating, 10.00 a.m. I did a search of the materials that we had found in the archive, and I found an identical order which, however, had something that most all of such orders had, a serial number, which appeared quite interesting since all of the orders and reports that I had seen by -- bearing the name of General Blaskic or Colonel Blaskic at the time, his practice of numbering, they were consecutive. In other words, beginning with 1 in a given month and simply go. This particular one, the number was surrounded by numbers from a different date, that date being what I took initially to be the 23rd of April. I subsequently located another document, logbook, listing or purporting to list communications coming out of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone headquarters, and the document or, rather, the order bearing that number in question 01-4-508 - I've looked at it many times and it stuck in my mind - appeared under the 23rd of April with the same subject line, addressees. I forget whether there were other criteria or other descriptive terms, but it did appear in that log under the 23rd. I subsequently found yet another version. This had been addressed -- the preparatory order in question had been addressed to a large number of recipients, as I recall, the brigades in the Operative Zone. So my thought was, well, a good place to look for it would be the incoming mail files of the different brigades and it did turn up in several of these. One included with it an order by a brigade commander of, as I recall, the Zrinjski Brigade, dated the 23rd of April and retyping at least the beginning of that particular report for issuance to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, before moving on, it may seem like a small point, but some lines ago or minutes ago now you talked about the date of this document. Just so the record is clear, when you say the 15th of April, you're talking about 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, 1993. The "15" was penned in or written in by hand over what was otherwise essentially an either typed or printed document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is there anything more that you can say about that comparison or the conclusion you reached about -- based on your analysis of these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The conclusion is not for the witness. But what we could have, Mr. Scott, is the exhibit number for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll ask -- provide that to you momentarily. I'm sorry. Are you talking about the order or the log that he's referring to or about, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can deal, first of all, with the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll provide it to you momentarily, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, according to the statement, it's Exhibit D3601, tab 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could check that to make sure we've got it right. As for the log, has that been produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's in the bundle of documents, and I was about to ask the witness two questions about that. Not in the bundle of documents because it's a thick document. It's separately produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, Mr. Prelec, can you help the Chamber in terms of the operating log that you used to compare the dates of these documents? To your knowledge, based on your involvement in these matters, that is one of the documents that's been collected and provided is to the Chamber as part of this exercise, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I have no idea of who it's been provided to. I really couldn't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fair enough. You're aware that in the last number of days that's one of the documents that's been collected?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think the Chamber will see that you have it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I do seem to recall confirming that it had been submitted. "Disclosed," I think, the term was, but I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you before moving on since we're on the topic of logbooks, in the course of your experience with this archival material or working with it, did you come across something that at least has been commonly referred to as the Blaskic diary or war diary?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one objection, Your Honour. I don't believe we've ever heard that document being referred to in this case, so it can't be commonly referred to as anything, and I don't believe I've seen it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'll rephrase it, Your Honour. It is so commonly referred by us but I take counsel's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come across an additional -- apart from the operational log you were testifying about a moment ago, sir, did you come across an additional journal or logbook type of material, a voluminous journal type of material as part of your work?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, I could provide some background on this. Yes, I found something that had a distinct title which I now don't recall exactly what that was, but since within the Office of the Prosecutor there had been a lot of discussion about -- and also not just within the office, in the Croatian media, a discussion about the so-called Blaskic diary, I asked Mr. Kulenovic in the archive to look for it. He said, he, you know, at that particular time would do so. But ultimately, yes, I did find a notebook which consisted of notes by the duty officer or purported to consist of notes by the duty officer in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. There was actually a series of these books. The one in question covered the early part of 1993; some parts in greater detail. The section which is one of the only ones I've actually read, the 16th of April, is in great detail, minute by minute. Other days are -- some days are simply skipped entirely or presented much more briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can hand you what's been marked as Exhibit Z610, 610.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hand that to Mr. Prelec, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the so-called war diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it's one of the documents that's been supplied to us but upon which we're going to have to rule --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- as part of the Zagreb materials aside from the schedules?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can certainly look at it but of course can't produce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My only question is: Is that -- do you recognise that as the document that you've been talking -- describing to the Chamber in the last five minutes, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where did you find -- where do you recall first seeing or coming across that document, you or those working with you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I found it myself in -- I forget the precise number of the box, but it was in the part of the HVO archive labelled as "ZP Vitez" collection. There were five or six boxes, each containing several notebooks or books or records of this type, and it was in one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could have your assistance again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to hand you what's been marked Exhibit Z351.2. If you'd just look at that for a moment. Let's just pause for the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. President, but I can't find this document on the many indices that we've been provided. Could the Prosecution just tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. It's the operating log. That's our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you, Mr. Prelec, looking at that document, in comparing these orders that you were talking a few minutes ago, you referred to another log, an operational log. Can you tell us whether the document that's been placed before you now is that log?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was, I think, in a different one of those boxes I had just referred to, four or five boxes, and it was accompanied by other logs for other date ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll try to move - Your Honours, I appreciate the Court's patience - and try to finish this before, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before changing topics a bit at the end of the statement here, can I ask you then -- I asked you earlier about the size of the collection. Is it fair to say that the size of the collection grew as the summer and fall progressed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I and -- I was told, yes, that it did grow. The last estimate that I received from the Croatian State Archive was expressed in linear length, which is an archival measurement indicating basically length on a shelf, and that was 4 linear kilometres worth of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let me now ask you to look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could help me again. Actually, it's the same bundle. I don't know if you still have the bundle or documents or not that we distributed earlier. If the witness could have those momentarily, please. It may be helpful -- Mr. Usher, if you could put each of these -- it may assist the Chamber, Your Honours, in reviewing these documents later, just to see what they look like visually. So just momentarily, if you could first put Exhibit 2834 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this appears to be an anonymous document, and it appears to be undated. Could we know the provenance of it and the putative date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel. 2834.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can start with that one if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Objection withdrawn, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 2834. Your Honour, this is a decision on the release of archival material to the Croatian State Archive. Again, I'm doing this primarily to identify visually for the Chamber, Your Honour, and then I'll ask the count -- I'll simply ask the witness to identify the manner which these documents were produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is the document to which we objected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is titled for the record "Documentation on the war in BiH", and I can tell the Chamber -- well, this was produced by the Office for Cooperation to the OTP in response to a request for assistance which we're free to -- we can certainly go into with the Chamber separately. It was specifically -- again, Your Honour, it was a request from the OTP for various reports about documents and this is one of the documents produced by the Republic of Croatia in response to that. The exhibit 2834.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Scott. Where does this document purport to come from? There is no indication on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can tell the Court that, if need be, I can produce information about the transmission of it to the Zagreb office of the ICTY by the Croatia Office for Cooperation. And if need be, I can also point the Chamber to the request to which it responds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what you are seeking to put in evidence here has no indication whatsoever as to its origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is exactly as we received it, Your Honour. I would be happy to address it separately outside this witness if the Chamber -- if it assists the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, is it -- I mean it's a history of what's happened about the production of this material, most of which we've heard about already. Given the doubt about where it comes from or the lack of evidence, it seems to me that it's not going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honour, this is some of that evidence. It isn't a lack of evidence. This tells -- provides the Chamber, these documents provides the Chamber produced by the State of Croatia in specific response to an Article 29 request from this Tribunal to provide information on these documents was presented for those purposes and to, in fact, ask some of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But now what we are having to determine is the admissibility of these documents. I will instruct Defence counsel that if there is any issue as to the availability of the documents, they must put the matter to this witness so that he can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there is no question to availability or there are no questions asked about it, then we shall assume that these -- the documents were not available and they have been made available subsequently. Meanwhile, I don't think we are assisted by this history.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. If I can just finish it then so that the witness doesn't have to be asked again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These four documents, 2834, 2834.1, 2834.2, and 2834.3, to your knowledge, sir, and I'm asking: Do you have a knowledge of these documents coming into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor from the State of Croatia and its agencies, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. The first three to which counsel referred I saw in my office and was told that they had been submitted by the Office for Cooperation. Document 2834.3 appears to be part of something that was given to me and I believe also Mr. Scott in the premises of the Croatian State Archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just direct your attention to this. The Chamber will see or has seen by now on the schedules of so-called Zagreb documents, there's the three: Kordic, Cerkez, and miscellaneous. In the interest of time, I won't even take the time to hand this out unless the Chamber wishes me to, but with represent to you, Mr. Prelec, that on that document, among other things is indicated as a source, that some of these documents came from something called the Croatian Government OFC, Office for Cooperation. And just so the Chamber is aware, how did the protection of those documents differ from the documents which are simply marked "HVO archive"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, the ones that are marked HVO archive are documents that were inspected, for the most part, inspected by either myself or one of my colleagues and copied at the Croatian State Archive or earlier in Samobor. They also include documents that were provided to us by the Office for Cooperation in -- but in one specific case, namely copies of documents selected by various defence teams also on the basis of work in the archive. The documents marked "OFC" are documents submitted in response to binding orders of this Chamber or another Chamber or requests for assistance to the Republic of Croatia, various orders and requests. Some of those appeared to be -- well, I shouldn't speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That's, I think, sufficient, subject to the Chamber's questions.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I could, I suppose, put it this way: Some documents that I have seen from that OFC category also appeared and were found by me in the HVO archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're at 1.00 as everyone can see on the clock. I'm in the Court's hands. I can probably finish in a couple of minutes whether you'd like me to finish immediately following the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, unless the Chamber has questions about that, I'm going to change to a separate category of documents very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just consult with Mr. Nice momentarily, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the next series of questions probably need to be in private session. We don't have to go into closed, but given the nature of this material -- the material, let me just tell the Chamber, that ultimately the material itself is not -- will not be protected but the -- some of the questions and the way in which it was accessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prelec, finally then, apart from the manner in which some of these materials were presented -- we're now back into public session -- I just want to ask you: Is Exhibit Z2833 a summary of transcripts received from the Office of the President of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to that, Your Honour. We've not received English language translations of most of these putative presidential transcripts. They consist of literally thousands of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to deal with the transcripts tomorrow at the earliest. We are going to deal with the other exhibits first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour, but this witness was prepared in identifying and preparing this summary. That's the reason I've asked him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got to adjourn now in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We are concluded, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, will you be back, please, in an hour and a half. We'll make it quarter to 3.00. Don't speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, did you write the statement dated October the 29th, 2000, yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you checked everything carefully before you actually wrote the statement, I take it, all of the facts?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I composed it myself. I sent it to Prosecution counsel. There were some suggested abbreviations and revisions. I checked it over to see if it accorded with my recollection and I'm confident it's correct, but I cannot claim to have gone back and checked each individual assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you read carefully the two specific documents that are referred to in the statement, the one that is described in paragraph 14, the Blaskic order of April the 15th, and the one in paragraph 11, the request for information sent by Colonel Blaskic to Mr. Cerkez on April the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct. I examined them carefully sometime prior to composing the statement, and I re-examined the former document after composing the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us that you are an historian by training and avocation, that you've been a teacher for several years, and for the last year and a half you've been an employee of the Prosecution, working as a research officer. Is that a fair summary of the state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in both capacities, you've had the opportunity to read original documents, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And with your academic training, you're taught to bring a fairly skeptical approach to documents, a cool, objective approach, testing the contents of those documents to ensure that they're internally consistent and externally consistent with information? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: It's a fairly broad statement. I'm not sure I would put it in precisely the same way. The historical profession does involve dealing with documents and assessing them critically. Perhaps I should simply put it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. But you are taught in your profession, I think, as you say, to assess documents critically and not merely to accept what they say on face value, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To quote a composer from our country, George Gershwin, "The things you are to liable read in the Bible, it ain't necessarily so." Would you agree with that in terms of documents that you come across in your profession, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, again if I could phrase it in a way that I'm somewhat more comfortable with, I don't think there are any historians that would assert that everything found in every document is necessarily true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's certainly true, you would concede, sir, in the case of documents whose authors we don't know, whose sources are not recited, and which contain conclusion and conjectures that are not based upon any identifiable documents? You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, once again, I'm somewhat uncomfortable discussing things at this level of generality, but I think one could draw a distinction between a document intended to produce a certain conclusion and a document that reports for other purposes certain facts. And, moreover, one thing that we are taught to do is to work with -- within imperfection and learn what we can from documentation that may not be wholly perfectly reliable because such things are -- one looks for such things often in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I agree. But you would concede, would you not, that if you come across an anonymous document and it contains what turns out to be very serious factual inaccuracies, just outright misstatements of facts, you would tend to treat that document, with your analytical skills as a historian, not particularly seriously; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: It would depend on the context. I think one would certainly be mistaken in accepting such a document at face value, but if it addressed the subject on which one had interest, one would, I think, be fully justified in attempting to confirm or refute the assertions made in such a document that that document alone would be inadequate to prove. That's the way I would -- and I have addressed such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Instead of revolving in the area of generality. Let's see if we can talk about some concrete matters, Mr. Prelec.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I can just ask the usher to put this document on the ELMO, this was previously marked as an exhibit D344/1, Tab 8. But it's just in the Croatian, Your Honours, and I just use this as a exemplar to make a point. Could you move it up to the signature line, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, here we have a document that appears to be signed by Colonel Blaskic. It has an official Central Bosnia Operative Zone or Travnik stamp, and official stamp. It's got on the bottom left-hand corner what appears to be a packet radio receipt stamp. If you just move to the top of the document, Mr. Usher. The document appears to have a correct number up at the top and although it's not an especially felicitous copy, it appears to be on Hrvatska Vijece Obrane Herceg-Bosna letterhead, and then it has on the top right-hand corner a stamp that you've identified as the Zagreb archival stamp; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. The only slightly peculiar thing is it seems to have been recopied from a -- possibly slightly reduced, but your description matches the appearance of the document as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And the only point I'm making is as you know with your background in Yugoslav history, the country has a rather long history of a bureaucratic tradition and documents like this bearing proper signatures, seals, and numbers are documents that you, as a historian, would tend to treat as authentic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. If I could introduce one qualification. There's also the factor of where the document is found. It's one thing to pick it up on the street. It's another -- the context is important, but I would concur with your statement. I would tend to value such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And my understanding from your testimony, Mr. Prelec, is that all documents that were produced to you, your colleagues, and your office had these archival stamps on the documents such as the one that we see here on the top right-hand corner of the document that's currently on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That actually wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the exception of the ad hoc copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the Samobor documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's true. But the Samobor documents were produced in May of this year, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My question was: All of the documents that were produced to you after June of this year following the Samobor episode, those documents were produced with the archival stamps on them with a few exceptions as you've described?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: The great majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say that you had 500 SIS binders or you saw 500 Security and Information Service binders. Were these Croatian -- Republic of Croatia SIS binders or Bosnia-Herzegovina SIS binders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I didn't actually physically see all 500 that I assume were in that room. When I say 500, there was like a catalogue listing 500. And to answer your question, they were the SIS of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also described a book or a document that's been marked as Exhibit Z610.1, and according to the spine of the document delivered to us, this is a book of observations of the officer on duty in the SB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could give you a copy of Exhibit 610.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you finished with the other exhibit, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, this is the logbook or however it's described?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. There is only one thing that I would like to draw to the Court's attention in considering this document, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could have it. In due course, we are going to have to consider the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. I hope this question will help you in that inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you would just turn to pages 22 and 23 of this document, sir, which purportedly record events at the end of January of 1993 between January 29th, 1993 and January 31st, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Excuse me, the copy that I've been handed doesn't have page numbers. Could you repeat the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. January 29th to January 31st.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Is this the correct page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's a page, page number 10, I believe, on the top of the Croatian version. Anyway, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, why don't we --

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could assist me. Oh, it's the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, could we have that on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, for this entry in January 1993 -- you speak Croatian, don't you, Mr. Prelec?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good. Could you just read the bold entry right in the middle of the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: In Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Or translate?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you can translate it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. "War diary from 15 04 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And how does it come that that entry is right in the middle of a page dealing with events in January 1993, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you made any inquiries along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. And, frankly, I wouldn't know where to start. It appears to have been written over something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you don't know who wrote it over something else or when, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document. It would be fair to say that you don't actually know who wrote the entries into this document, do you? Right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Partly correct. They are written in what appear to me several different hands, and there are some names scattered throughout and including, I believe, at the end, of persons who are familiar to me, but at this point, I could not tell you who wrote the individual entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that you've not spoken to anybody who has personal knowledge of that document and can tell you what it is and when it was written?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the Prosecution has had access to so-called Zagreb documents, I believe, or at least some, 20 boxes or so, 20 binders, since May the 2nd this year, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That was when our access began, as I described it much more fully in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And there is no question that following the move of these documents to the Croatian State Archive, access to the Prosecution to these documents has been granted on a preferential basis, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how I could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I'm just reading from the third page of --

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: In fact, I would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Z2834.1, this anonymous document that the Prosecution has made reference to, and it says: "The Defence of all indicted Central Bosnia Croats examined about 30 binders. Less than 500 pages of documents were copied and given to the Defence teams, even though more were requested. The reason for this imbalance is that the ICTY Prosecution requested and received priority in examining documents." Is that an accurate statement of fact, Mr. Prelec?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I really can't address the degree to which various Defence teams had access beyond what I testified to earlier today because I have no knowledge of that beyond, again, having seen individual members present at the archive and having been told in very general terms by Mr. Zunec.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that the imbalance recited in this document is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The document also goes on to recite on the first page, under the "Delivery of Material" section, that materials arrived at the Croatian Information Service in two deliveries, one in July of 1996, when about 200 crates of material were delivered, and the second in April of 1999 when a truckload of material was delivered and stored in a hallway. Now, can you throw any light on what documents were delivered to the Croatian Information Service in July of 1996, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. I would assume that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is no need to assume.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You know or you don't?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the same is true of the documents assertedly delivered, this truckload of documents in April of 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. You don't know what documents were delivered to the Croatian Information Service, or HIS, in a truck in April of 1999, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And these documents, according to this record anyway, were delivered. They arrived in a state of disarray, without any kind of register, and then exchange receipt was not made in either case. Now, you say that you saw a list of documents or some sort of an archival index that assisted you in selecting particular documents of interest to you, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And could you tell us who prepared that index and when?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, the one that I used was prepared or I was told it was prepared by the staff of the archive, the Croatian State Archive, subsequent to the arrival of the documents though, they did have some fairly rudimentary indices that had been prepared earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: My understanding is Mr. Dvor Marijin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have no reason to believe though that the facts recited in this document, Z2834.1, to the effect that these documents arrived in a state of disarray without any kind of register, is incorrect, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. I have no reason to believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please make a break between the answer and the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- have been of assistance to you. They've tried to help you in every way turning around requests for copying in a very expeditious way. I think you said that in your direct examination, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I did refer to several instances. I would not be correct in making that as a general statement. There was enormous variability in these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you're being asked to have a break between question and answer, and, of course, between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are some times when I can't just help myself, but I will do my best to exercise some self-restraint here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, it would be fair to say, would it not, that you and your team saw these documents for the first time this year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, there were some -- it depends on how you mean "document." There were copies of same of the documents that had been obtained in other means, several that I can think of. There was, I understand, a seizure operation in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm talking about the archival documents that you examined in May and June and thereafter. The point is, those particular documents were produced to you in the order in which they were produced for the first time this year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you really don't have the slightest idea of how many people have had access to the component parts of these documents during the last six and a half years, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, for some periods of time, the document to which you referred earlier had some comments that no one had access, but it doesn't cover the entire time period. So I suppose the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. You can't tell whether documents have actually been added to the archive or subtracted from it, can you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You can't tell, in fact, sir, that this is indeed the so-called HVO archive, can you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I'm certain it is. I don't know in what degree of detail you'd like me to pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Security and Information Service in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina had access to these files before they were produced to you during the six and a half years before you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: The Security -- the SIS of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, since the archive itself did make reference to that service, at least that service in Bosnia-Herzegovina, having those documents and there was correspondence between them and the sister service in Croatia, I could indicate that insofar as those documents are correct, that they did have access, at least at some periods of time. But personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you, have you seen documents that would indicate that the SIS, the Bosnian Croat SIS component of this archive was actually moved around to Bosnia-Herzegovina by the people in charge of that agency in Mostar, Ivica Lucic being one of them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: There were references -- at this point, the only reference that I recall is to a removal from Bosnia-Herzegovina in what appeared to be the summer of 1997, and there was a document indicating an imminent planned move in May, but also the document that you referred to earlier indicated arrival of some documents in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're not aware, for example, of Mr. Lucic breaking up the SIS archive and moving it to various locations in the country outside of Mostar assertedly to keep it out of the hands of a man by the name of Mladen Naletelic also, I believe, known as Tuta?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. I really don't know anything about that and generally know relatively little about the activities of Mr. Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, sir, you can't say that the so-called Service for Protection of Constitutional Order, the SZUP, the Ministry of the Interior, MUP, and the operatives of the Croatian Information Service, you can't tell whether they had actually been provided access to all of the documents that were given to you earlier this year in the intervening six and a half years since apparently some of them, anyway, were generated?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I couldn't speak to the first two instances you mentioned; however, I would simply recall my earlier testimony as to custody of the documents by the Croatian Information Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, have you ever seen any logbooks that show who has in fact had access to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we were shown a recently-produced document; it's been marked as Z2834.2, one of the documents that the Prosecution's referred to. Did you know that this so-called archival material was not transferred directly to Zagreb, it was stored in a facility, a military facility in Split called Lora?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen multiple references to at least some of the material having been stored in the facility to which you refer, the port, the military port of Lora. My assumption has been that at least one, probably two shipments were stored there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You've read the letter I've dated November 9th, 2000 from Major Cindy Radic sent to the Office for Cooperation with the ICTY, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I have read that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could just put this on the ELMO. Thank you. Start with page one in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This document states that a large amount of HVO archival material is located in the military complex Lora. Do you know, sir, what kinds of archival material are located in this facility?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. Excuse me, could you refer me once again to where in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the first paragraph right in the middle. It says, "A large amount of HVO archival material is located in the military complex Lora."

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: My impression is that I could consult the Croatian language. It seems to indicate that this was a past event since it refers immediately thereafter to a decision in March. We did have discussions with various representatives of government of Croatia that mentioned material in Lora in addition to the material in the custody of the Ministry of Defence as represented as two different issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. But you've never been down to Lora to take a look at what it is. The custodians of those documents actually have in their possession; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. I tried to persuade the OTP to send me down there in the summertime, but they, for reasons unknown to me, declined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The letter goes on to say, "The material was stored in eight offices without any systematic arrangement and was in absolute disorder." You've got no reason to disagree with that characterisation of the way these records were kept; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I really couldn't comment. I have no firsthand or other hand knowledge of conditions in Lora.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact the author goes on to say that operatives in the Split department stated that in the time from the original storing of this materials, nobody accessed it and this was indicated by the state in which it was found completely disarrayed.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: If you would allow me to amend my previous answer. At a meeting with an assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, I and several others were shown another set of photographs prepared, he said, by the military police of various documents held in various places in Croatia. Some of these were prefaced by photographs indicating Split as the location so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So your understanding is that there was documents all over the place?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: At several location. They did not appear, and this is in response to your earlier question, and this is the reason for the correction, they appeared to have been stored in cabinets, what appeared to be metallic cabinets, again in binders. Disorder, I think, would perhaps be too strong a term although there's no way to tell from the photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the second page, second paragraph. The author of this document, after stating on page one that there was no list of any material found just as in the first document we looked at, states that the idea of coming up with a list cropped up but it wasn't feasible because of the short time frame, the disorder of the material, and the very poor physical state of the material caused by poor storage, being exposed to high temperatures, humidity, and rodents.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Mice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you've got no reason to believe that that description of the storage conditions is not completely accurate, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I can't go beyond my previous answer as to what I assume is a subset of storage conditions which I saw photographically. The documents that -- no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And once again, you cannot tell us who has had access to those documents during the time that they have been residing in Lora?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Or anywhere else these documents are located. Wherever those locations are, the same is true. You do not know who has had access to those documents or for how long?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Those are all military facilities. In my earlier reference, they weren't at a random, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next document that you were asked to identify for us was a letter supposedly written by Dr. Josip Kulenovic and he describes the state of affairs on page two. He being, I believe, the director of the state archives?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He tells us that, "The material was located in a hallway of the archival storage. Nobody knew what to say about the type or amount of material involved. A large portion of the material was found in a state of disarray with," he says, "the exception being that part of the material of the command of the Vitez formation area and individual subordinate units." You've no reason to disagree with that characterisation of the manner in which this material was kept, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, I'm somewhat hampered. I have seen that letter but I have not read it as opposed to the others. But from what you read now, I suppose it's not a surprise that the Vitez material was in some shape by the time he received it, since prior to that it had been accessed by us and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I'll come back to that. But on page six of this letter, Mr. Kulenovic, the state archivist, goes on to say that the military police documents were thrown about without chronological or thematic order. You've got no reason to believe that that's not the case, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, as it turns out, the very first binders I saw when I went with Dr. Kulenovic to inspect the archive were military police, and they seemed to be in order, but I really can't help you even if I could, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And you don't know whether it was Mr. Kulenovic himself who had imposed order out of chaos and actually put those documents into the order and state in which they were produced to you, do you sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I would have no reason to believe he had, but again I can't provide positive information on that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are asked to break after your questions and after the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, these materials from the Department of Defence, the HZ HB and HR HB Department of Defence or Ministry of Defence were stuffed into binders without thematic order according to Mr. Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Once again, I have not read this but I can say that something that appears to be similar to or identical to the material to which you refer was shown to me briefly in a meeting by Mr. Kulenovic as material he had received upon receipt of the HVO archive and to which I referred earlier in my statement that there was some rudimentary description that had been prepared prior to the catalogues prepared by the archive. The reason I bring this up is if that's the case, then it would be misleading to refer to this as a statement of Mr. Kulenovic's; it would rather be a communication by Mr. Kulenovic of someone else's statement, presumably Mr. Marijin's. But without further examination, and at least a reading of this, I couldn't, again, say to what degree it's an accurate description of what was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. But when the HIS materials were transferred over to the Zagreb archive, it was Mr. Kulenovic who received those materials actually and not you, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, he was the head of the institution. I don't know who actually received them. I doubt it was him but, yes, it was his institution and not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it was only after the institution, the archives had received these materials, processed them, organised them, and so forth that they were produced to you; right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, the organisation process had only just begun when we began working with the documents and it continued in parallel. So my understanding was that not very much had been done by the time we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any HZ HB or any HR HB regulations dealing with how documents were supposedly admitted to any HVO archives? How they were dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: There were references. There were binders that I saw listed in the catalogue that referred to handover of archival materials from one custodian to another, but the pressure -- the time pressure I was under was enormous, and I thought the likelihood of finding relevant material there was small. There were a large number of these binders. So to precisely answer your question, I did see reference to such a thing, but I did not see the thing itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many locations in which the records of the HZ HB and HR HB were originally kept, official records of either of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Do you mean -- could you be more specific, please? The central government or what particular organ?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's just take, for example, the Department of Defence of the HZ HB. Where did the Department of Defence actually keep its records, Mr. Prelec? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. My assumption would be initially they would keep them in their offices and then they would be transferred to another location that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's an assumption and you just don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the same is true for the Department of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That would be easy to find out since it would be a matter of legislation, but I don't know offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you yourself ever spoken to anybody, any official of the Croatian Information Service about these documents other than Mr. Ozren Zunec earlier this year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And who?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I can't tell you his name. It was very peculiar. I had dealings with this gentleman on several occasions, and he steadfastly refused to reveal his name, even when a colleague of mine went up and introduced himself. So I simply don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever met anyone from a body known as the SIS centar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you don't know where the SIS centar documents, if they ever existed, were kept, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, my understanding is there were multiple SIS centars, but with that qualification, I have no personal knowledge of where they were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: If we're referring to the same thing. I assume we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. You simply don't know where those documents were located if they ever existed, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by "if they ever existed," but -- since I did see them, but beyond that, do I know where they were located? Beyond what I said in my direct examination, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You have never met with a man by the name of Miso Mijic or Dragan Voloder, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a quick look at the Viteska Brigade issues, if my colleague will forgive me for pre-empting him for a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One document I'd like to have marked as an exhibit is the transmittal memorandum from Orsat Miljenic to the ICTY in May of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any objection to this document being produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be numbered D346/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've seen this document before, I take it, Mr. Prelec.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And this is dated six months ago, sir. It describes 15 categories of documents, and 11 of those categories deal with the Viteska Brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That appears to be the case. I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you say that you saw all sorts of binders with "Viteska Brigade" listed on the spines, and you asked for copies of those documents and they were given to you six months ago, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, yes, these particular documents, on the order forms, reflected -- this is where it says the PPIZD1 and then numbers, yes. Those documents would have been provided and I believe were provided along with this form in late May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Six months ago.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Approximately six months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, one part of your statement I'd like to cover with you is paragraph 11. Let me just read it to you. Do you have your statement with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And it's the second sentence that I'm interested in. You say one document in particular caught your attention, which was a request for information sent by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic to Mario Cerkez on 16 of April, 1993, recently marked as Exhibit Z692.2. "The document requested information about the Viteska Brigade's progress in four Central Bosnian villages, including Ahmici and Donja Veceriska."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I could just ask the usher to put this document on the ELMO. This is Exhibit Z692.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now this document doesn't mention Ahmici or Donja Veceriska, does it, Mr. Prelec, anywhere except on the back in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So, in fact, Colonel Blaskic was not asking Mr. Cerkez about the Viteska Brigade's progress in four Central Bosnian villages, including Ahmici and Donja Veceriska, was he, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I could not agree with you. He is asking for a report on the current situation "in your zone of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Which you have stated in more specific terms, as did I in point 11 of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I'm just using the words that you used in your statement, sir, and I don't mean to quibble with you or argue, but the document says, "Zone of responsibility," and it doesn't say "four Central Bosnian villages including Ahmici and Donja Veceriska," does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we're helped by this. This is a matter of argument. You can address this to us in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second point of interest on this document, sir, that you highlighted and said you'd never forget, is in pencil on the back side of this document. There were some notes written, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And when were those notes written?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: How could I possibly know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And you don't know who wrote them either, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. I believe I made that clear in my direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second document that you referred to is Exhibit D306/1 tab 102, which was an exhibit in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have this put on the ELMO, please. The Croatian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if we could just take a look at the top of the document, the date of it, which has been asserted to be the 15th of April, 1993. Let me just suggest to you, Mr. Prelec, that someone has crudely altered the date of this document in handwriting, and you can see it. It leaps out at you. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: The date has been altered in hand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that's sort of an example then of a document that bears one state or one asserted species of information that ain't necessarily so; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I was waiting for the French translation to conclude. The -- if you refer to the "15," yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, is there anything else in the document which you say has been altered apart from the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have no reason, Your Honour, to dispute what the -- what the witness says and that is that this document actually appears in a different register in a different date. The reason that we included this in our exhibits was not necessarily to attest to the accuracy of the date but merely to show, if this really needed to be shown, the hundreds and hundreds of orders that the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic, issued, this being one of them. But I have absolutely no reason to dispute the testimony of the witness. And we can see it for ourselves that this date appears to have been deliberately altered by someone or altered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the final topic about which you testified, Mr. Prelec, the transcripts of conversations that assertedly occurred in the office of the President of the Republic of Croatia over a period of years that have been produced apparently in abundance to your office earlier this year. We know that from your testimony, you said in the LiveNote on page 60 today, that you saw a tape that was dated 1991 and that this tape had been kept apparently because it was felt to be historically important. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: That was my assumption. The precise date on the tape was late March 1991, and it was a recording where it appeared to be -- the date corresponded to the date of a meeting of most or all of the Yugoslav republic presidents. They were having a series of these meetings. It initially caught my eye because it was a tape, and I had been looking for material on the Karadjordjevo meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you, sir, but pressure of time is upon us, and the only question was this tape that you saw was from 1991, yes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And had a transcript been made of this tape that was subsequently provided to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: We were provided a transcript of the meeting that I assumed that tape to have recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So as early as 1991, the office of the president was making decisions that tapes should actually be retained if they were felt to have an historical importance?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I can't comment on that. I have no information to -- that would allow me to make such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The transcripts that have been provided by the -- or to you by the Prosecution to us, I think that you said you did not, except with one recent concession, have listened to any of the original tapes themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: No. I've listened to no recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And your understanding -- and your understanding is that the tapes themselves have been reused? Is that what you are given to believe?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: This is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So there is no way to check the accuracy of the transcripts themselves, is there, by now?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, it's impossible to check them against the tape. It would be possible to examine other or to explore other avenues establishing their accuracy, to explore the process by which the transcripts were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But there's just no way right now to be sure that these are accurate transcriptions of what the tapes assertedly contained, is there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Again, I don't see what you're asking beyond what I've said. One cannot check them against the original since the original does not exist, against the tape, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello, Mr. Prelec. My name is Bozidar Kovacic and together with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, I'm a Defence counsel for the accused Mario Cerkez. I will ask my questions in Croatian and so I would please ask you to observe the requisite pause between the question and answer. My colleague already asked some questions that I was going to ask, but I do have further questions. You mentioned in your curriculum vitae that you had an opportunity to work in the archive in Vienna, in Washington, D.C., and in other places. Could you please, in two sentences tell us, I suppose, that the documents that you have examined in the state archive in Zagreb with respect -- as compared to the documents that you have seen previously in your work in Vienna or D.C.? I suppose that these documents differ quite a lot from what you were used to based on your previous experiences.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I would have to say that the material I reviewed in Zagreb which was some of the most exciting and rewarding material I had the chance to review in my professional career was largely similar to material I had reviewed in other archives except that I knew far more of its origin and could be far more confident in it than is normally the case in historical research. There were differences since the material I looked at in Washington, for example, related to the early 1970s. In Vienna, the 1900s handwritten in German. So -- but it would not strike, it did not strike me as peculiar from an archival point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Documents that you were given in Zagreb, the state archive itself, you said that the archive started working on the documents basically at the same time when you started working. And as the time progressed, this was expanded in the sense of creating reference lists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: They had begun slightly before we began and had done some work, but my impression is that most of their work took place, as you say, while we were working there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the archive in Zagreb, when you were given a certain document, certain binder from the archive, any binder, you were, perhaps, the first one or the second or the fifth one to ever see this document. Perhaps some of the Defence counsels had access or somebody from this Tribunal had access to this document, but other than that, there were no other researchers who had access to these documents; isn't that correct? It was only the people from this Tribunal, the Defence counsels and the Prosecutors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, will you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While you worked in the archives in Zagreb, have you ever seen any other historians, researchers, or other people who had access to this material? Have you, based on -- you told us a lot about the archive, its organisation. Were you able to conclude, based on what you have known, that other researchers prior to you had access to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, occasionally we would mark the documents with a yellow adhesive paper, and on several occasions, I found pieces like this in a binder that none of my colleagues recognised. I can't say where they come from, possibly the Defence, possibly someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, bearing in mind everything that you were able to find out about when the documents arrived physically in the archive and when you, as well as other people from this Tribunal started examining these documents, do you believe that there was a significant number of other people who came to archive before you and examined these documents prior to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Insofar as your question relates to the archive, the Croatian State Archive, my impression is that no other persons, aside from the OTP and the Defence and members of the government of Croatia had access to that collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you would take -- when you would take a specific document in an archive in D.C., would you say that you were among the first 20 people to ever hold that document in your hands, if I can paraphrase my question? Is it likely that any document that you laid your hands on in Vienna or anywhere else was prior to you seen by a great number of other researchers or other people who had access to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't follow the question. What is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to lay a foundation to the disarray in the archive, and the witness stated in his first question that he saw no difference between an archive in Zagreb and Washington. I wanted to say that the documents in D.C. had been examined because hundreds of thousands of researchers have seen these documents before that, and there was literature or research paperwork to confirm this whereas in Zagreb, these documents had arrived into archive a week before they had been seen for the first time. So there has been no evaluation of this raw material, and this is one of the points that I am trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, you've heard what counsel has said. Can you assist us by preparing the material you saw in Zagreb with material you've seen elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Normally, one does not -- historian does not look at archival material that has been looked at by large numbers of other people; one looks for new material. It's the essence of discovery. So I am certain that in some cases, I did, in my professional career, look at material that had been seen by others, but not by very large numbers of others. Had that been the case, I would not have looked at it. Beyond that, the experience was quite similar as a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think possibly the point that counsel was seeking was the state of the archive. How did the state of the materials compare?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: They were not outside the norm of archival collections. Some collections are much better organised. In Washington, I worked in presidential papers and those were fairly rigorously maintained, but many of the other materials I had looked at, for example, in Ljubljana, I examined some court papers from the early years of this century that were in a significantly greater state of disarray than the HVO materials. This is why I say it's well within the range of order that a historian or that I as a historian have encountered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you for helping, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents pertaining to Viteska Brigade, would you please confirm for me some issues. I'm not sure that it is all clear. My first question is the following: Is it true that the documents of Viteska Brigade were found in various sets among those binders that you mentioned or were you given all of these documents together at the same place from A to Z?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: They were found in various places, many in the collection of the brigade itself, but several other places as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They were also among the set that has not been classified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Well, they were in the boxes that I referred to earlier that had come from the Ministry of Defence and those were simply labelled, "Vitez Operational Zone, Various Units." I didn't consult any completely unclassified material. We were -- it would be pointless. The quantity was too large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This very collection that came from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and which contained various documents of the operational zone, the documents that you referred as being a set of documents pertaining to the middle of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that among this collection, among this pile, folders that came from the Ministry of Defence, you were able to determine that this came from SIS, the information agency? Did you inquire in which part of the Ministry of Defence these documents were kept, who released them into the archive? Are you stating this was not obvious from any of the material that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC
